title: Digital Circuits & Radiated Emissions
description: The spectrum of digital signals, ground noise, loop and cable radiation, and how layout, edges and filtering keep a product under the limits.

study.title: Spectrum of a digital signal
study.body: A clock is a trapezoidal wave: amplitude $A$, pulse width $\tau$, rise time $t_r$, period $T$. Its harmonics lie under an envelope that is flat at $2A\tau/T$ up to $f_1 = 1/(\pi\tau)$, falls at **−20 dB/decade** up to $f_2 = 1/(\pi t_r)$ and at **−40 dB/decade** beyond. So the **rise time**, not the clock frequency, sets the high-frequency content; Ott takes $1/(\pi t_r)$ as the bandwidth of a logic signal (close to the familiar $0.35/t_r$). A 50 % square wave has only odd harmonics, the fundamental being $0.64A$.

study.title: Ground noise and the return path
study.body: Each switching gate draws a transient current (charging load capacitance plus 50–100 mA of shoot-through) that flows through the ground and supply inductance: $V = L\,di/dt$. A PCB trace has about 15 nH per inch (≈ 6 nH/cm) of loop inductance, far more important than its resistance at nanosecond edges; a plane has about 100× less, and decoupling capacitors next to each IC supply the charge locally. The **return current** takes the path of least resistance at DC, but above a few hundred kHz the path of least **inductance**: in the plane directly under the trace, which gives the smallest loop.

study.title: Differential-mode (loop) radiation
study.body: The normal signal current $I_{dm}$ flowing around a loop of area $A$ is a small loop antenna. Measured at distance $r$ over a reflecting ground plane (as in an emission test) the far field is at most the value below ($f$ in Hz, $A$ in m², $I$ in A, $r$ in m; at 3 m the constant becomes $87.6\times10^{-16}$). Field ∝ $f^2 A I$: **halving the loop area gives −6 dB, doubling the frequency +12 dB**. Valid while the loop perimeter is under $\lambda/4$. Example: 25 mA at 30 MHz in 10 cm² gives about 200 µV/m at 3 m, twice the Class B limit.

study.title: Common-mode (cable) radiation
study.body: Ground noise drives a small **common-mode** current $I_{cm}$ onto every attached cable (length $L$), which then acts as a monopole antenna. It is far more efficient than a loop: 1 m of cable needs about 1000× less current than a 10 cm² loop for the same field at 50 MHz. Only about **5 µA** at 50 MHz on a 1 m cable reaches the Class B limit (100 µV/m at 3 m). Above the frequency where the cable is $\lambda/4$ long, use $L = \lambda/4$ ($E \approx 94.5\,I_{cm}/r$). No $I_{cm}$ is needed for the circuit to work, so it is the designer's control knob.

study.title: Explore: emission envelopes
study.body: Model: a 25 MHz, 20 mA clock in a loop of area $A$, and a 1 m cable carrying 0.1 % of the clock current as common mode, both at 3 m, against the FCC Class B limit. Loop radiation ($f^2$) rises **+20 dB/dec** up to $f_2$ and then stays flat; cable radiation ($f$) is flat and falls above $f_2$ (and above $\lambda/4$). So common-mode radiation dominates at the lower frequencies and differential-mode at the higher ones; a smaller loop moves the crossover up. Slowing the edges ($t_r$) helps both.

study.title: Reducing emissions
study.body:
- **Loop area**: route clocks first, short, next to a solid plane; on two-layer boards give clocks a ground trace on **both** sides (canceling loops, 20+ dB).
- **Edges and frequency**: use the slowest rise time that works; a small series resistor (≈ 33 Ω) in clock outputs damps ringing.
- **Spread-spectrum (dithered) clock**: frequency-modulate the clock by ≈ 0.5–2 %; peaks drop 10–14 dB for **both** DM and CM.
- **Cables**: low ground impedance, common-mode chokes/ferrites, filter capacitors to the **chassis**, shields with a 360° connection to the enclosure, circuit ground bonded to chassis in the I/O area.

study.title: PCB layout and stackup
study.body: Return-path discontinuities force large loops (+20 dB): never route a fast trace over a **slot or split** in its reference plane (if unavoidable, place a stitching capacitor at the crossing); when a signal changes layers, add a ground-to-ground **stitching via** (or a power–ground capacitor) right next to it. Stackup objectives: every signal layer next to a plane, signal-to-plane spacing small (≤ 0.25 mm), power and ground planes close together, fast signals buried between planes, multiple ground planes; four or six layers cannot meet them all, and the first two always come first. A four-layer board is typically 20 dB quieter than a two-layer one.

steps.title: Spectrum of a clock
steps.body: A trapezoidal clock (pulse width $\tau$, rise time $t_r$) has harmonics under an envelope with two corners: −20 dB/decade from $f_1 = 1/(\pi\tau)$ and −40 dB/decade from $f_2 = 1/(\pi t_r)$. Above $f_2$ the energy is small, so $1/(\pi t_r)$ is the signal's bandwidth.

steps.prompt: A {{f0|Hz}} clock with 50 % duty cycle has rise and fall times of {{tr|s}}.

ask.prompt: Find the frequency $f_2$ above which its harmonics fall at 40 dB/decade.
ask.explanation: $f_2 = \frac{1}{\pi t_r}$ = 1/(π × {{tr|s}}) = **{{1/(pi*tr)|Hz}}**. This is also the bandwidth of the signal.

ask.prompt: Find the frequency $f_1$ where the envelope starts to fall at 20 dB/decade.
ask.explanation: The pulse width is half the period: $\tau = \frac{1}{2f_0}$ = {{1/(2*f0)|s}}. $f_1 = \frac{1}{\pi\tau}$ = **{{2*f0/pi|Hz}}** (below the fundamental, so all harmonics lie on the sloping parts).

steps.prompt: The clock frequency is doubled while the rise time stays the same. What happens to the spectral envelope?
options: $f_1$ doubles, $f_2$ stays the same
Both $f_1$ and $f_2$ double
$f_2$ doubles, $f_1$ stays the same
Nothing changes
steps.explanation: $f_1 = 1/(\pi\tau)$ depends on the pulse width, which halves; $f_2 = 1/(\pi t_r)$ depends only on the edges. The high-frequency content (above $f_2$) is set by the rise time, which is why fast logic is noisy even at a low clock rate.

steps.prompt: Slow the edges of this 10 MHz clock: set the rise time so that the −40 dB/decade corner lies at {{f2t|Hz}}.
steps.explanation: $f_2 = \frac{1}{\pi t_r}$, so $t_r = \frac{1}{\pi f_2}$ = 1/(π × {{f2t|Hz}}) = **{{trt|s}}**. Every harmonic above the corner is then lower than with faster edges.

steps.title: Ground bounce
steps.body: When outputs switch, the transient current flows through the inductance of the ground pins and traces. With nanosecond edges even a few nH matter, and outputs switching together add their currents. The resulting ground noise upsets logic and, more often, drives common-mode current onto cables.

steps.prompt: {{N}} outputs of an IC switch simultaneously, each with a current step of {{dI|A}} in {{tr|s}}. They share a ground inductance of {{L|H}}. Estimate the ground bounce voltage.
steps.explanation: $di/dt$ = {{N}} × {{dI|A}} / {{tr|s}} = {{N*dI/tr*1e-9||3}} A/ns. $V = L\,di/dt$ = {{L|H}} × {{N*dI/tr*1e-9||3}} A/ns = **{{L*N*dI/tr|V}}** (nH × A/ns gives volts directly).

steps.prompt: A ground trace has {{L|H}} of loop inductance. Find its reactance at the bandwidth $1/(\pi t_r)$ of a logic signal with $t_r$ = {{tr|s}}.
steps.explanation: $f = \frac{1}{\pi t_r}$ = {{1/(pi*tr)|Hz}}. $X_L = 2\pi fL$ = 2π × {{1/(pi*tr)|Hz}} × {{L|H}} = **{{2*L/tr|Ω}}** (simply $2L/t_r$), thousands of times the trace's DC resistance.

steps.title: Where the return current flows
steps.body: At DC the return current in a ground plane takes the path of **least resistance**: straight between the two vias. Above a few hundred kHz it takes the path of **least inductance**: concentrated directly under the signal trace, because that encloses the smallest loop. Anything that blocks this path (a slot, a split, a layer change without a nearby return via) makes the loop larger.

steps.prompt: A 100 MHz clock trace runs over a solid ground plane from one via to another along an L-shaped route. Its return current flows in a straight line between the two vias.
steps.explanation: That is the DC (least-resistance) path. At 100 MHz the return current follows the path of least inductance: underneath the trace, along its L-shaped route, which keeps the loop area minimal.

steps.prompt: Which of these increases the loop area of a fast signal's return path the most?
options: Routing the trace across a slot in the adjacent ground plane
Adding a ground stitching via next to the signal via
Placing the decoupling capacitor right at the IC
Routing the trace on a layer adjacent to a solid plane
steps.explanation: A slot forces the return current to detour around its ends, so the loop grows with the slot length (Ott measured up to 5× more ground voltage for a 1.5 inch slot). The other three options all keep the return path short and close to the signal.

steps.title: Two radiation models
steps.body: Differential mode: a loop of area $A$ carrying $I_{dm}$ (formula below). Common mode: a cable of length $L$ (shorter than $\lambda/4$) carrying $I_{cm}$: $E_{cm} = 12.6\times10^{-7}\,fLI_{cm}/r$. Both give the maximum far field at distance $r$ over a ground plane, in V/m with SI units. Fields in dBµV/m: $20\log_{10}(E/1\,\mu\text{V/m})$; the Class B limit at 3 m is 100 µV/m (40 dBµV/m) below 88 MHz.

steps.prompt: A {{I|A}} current at {{f|Hz}} flows around a loop of {{Acm}} cm² on a PCB. The field is measured at {{r}} m over a ground plane.

ask.prompt: Find the maximum electric field strength.
Find the maximum field strength in dBµV/m.

steps.prompt: A clock harmonic of {{I|A}} at {{f|Hz}} must stay below the Class B limit of 100 µV/m at 3 m. Find the largest allowed loop area, in cm².
steps.explanation: Solve $E = 263\times10^{-16}\frac{f^2AI}{r}$ for $A$: $A = \frac{Er}{263\times10^{-16}f^2I}$ = (100×10⁻⁶ × 3) / (263×10⁻¹⁶ × ({{f|Hz}})² × {{I|A}}) = {{Am||3}} m² = **{{Ac||3}} cm²**. That is a very small loop.

steps.prompt: A sinusoidal loop current keeps its amplitude, but the loop area is multiplied by {{a}} and the frequency by {{b}}. By how many dB does the differential-mode field change? (Increase positive, decrease negative.)
steps.explanation: $E \propto f^2A$, so the field ratio is $a\,b^2$ = {{a}} × {{b}}² = {{a*b^2||3}}. In dB: 20 log({{a*b^2||3}}) = **{{20*log10(a*b^2)||3}} dB** (area: 20 log {{a}} = {{20*log10(a)||3}} dB; frequency: 40 log {{b}} = {{40*log10(b)||3}} dB).

steps.prompt: A {{L}} m cable carries a common-mode current of {{Icm|A}} at {{f|Hz}}. The field is measured at {{r}} m.

ask.prompt: Find the maximum electric field strength.
ask.explanation: The cable is shorter than $\lambda/4$ = {{75e6/f||3}} m, so $E = 12.6\times10^{-7}\frac{fLI_{cm}}{r}$ = 12.6×10⁻⁷ × {{f|Hz}} × {{L}} m × {{Icm|A}} / {{r}} m = **{{E|V/m}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the maximum field strength in dBµV/m.

steps.prompt: Find the largest common-mode current allowed on a {{L}} m cable at {{f|Hz}} if the field at 3 m must stay below 100 µV/m.
steps.explanation: $I_{cm} = \frac{Er}{12.6\times10^{-7}fL}$ = (100×10⁻⁶ × 3) / (12.6×10⁻⁷ × {{f|Hz}} × {{L}}) = **{{100e-6*3/(12.6e-7*f*L)|A}}**. A few microamps: compare that with the milliamps of signal current on the same cable.

steps.prompt: For the same field strength, how many times larger must a differential-mode current in a {{Acm}} cm² loop be than a common-mode current on a {{L}} m cable, at {{f|Hz}}?
steps.explanation: Set the two fields equal: $263\times10^{-16}f^2AI_{dm} = 12.6\times10^{-7}fLI_{cm}$, so $\frac{I_{dm}}{I_{cm}} = \frac{12.6\times10^{-7}L}{263\times10^{-16}fA}$ = **{{12.6e-7*L/(263e-16*f*Acm*1e-4)||3}}**. Common-mode radiation is by far the more efficient mechanism.

steps.prompt: The rise time of a clock is increased from {{tr1|s}} to {{k*tr1|s}}. By how many dB does the emission envelope drop at {{fx|Hz}} (above both $1/\pi t_r$ corners)?
steps.explanation: Above $f_2 = 1/(\pi t_r)$ the current envelope is $\propto f_1f_2/f^2$, so at a fixed frequency it is proportional to $f_2 \propto 1/t_r$ (for both DM and CM radiation). Slowing the edges {{k}}× lowers it by 20 log {{k}} = **{{20*log10(k)||3}} dB**.

steps.prompt: On a four-layer board, the dielectric between each signal layer and its reference plane is reduced from {{h1}} mm to {{h2}} mm (same routing).

ask.prompt: By how many dB does the differential-mode (loop) radiation drop?
ask.explanation: The loop area of each trace is its length × its height above the plane, so $A$ drops by {{h1/h2||3}}×. $E \propto A$: 20 log {{h1/h2||3}} = **{{20*log10(h1/h2)||3}} dB**.

ask.prompt: Crosstalk between adjacent traces scales with the square of the trace height. By how many dB does it drop?
ask.explanation: Crosstalk $\propto h^2$: ratio ({{h1/h2||3}})² = {{(h1/h2)^2||3}}, i.e. 40 log {{h1/h2||3}} = **{{40*log10(h1/h2)||3}} dB**, at no extra cost.

steps.prompt: A ferrite with {{Zf|Ω}} impedance at the frequency of interest is clamped on a cable. The rest of the common-mode loop has an impedance of {{Zl|Ω}}. By how many dB does the common-mode current drop?
steps.explanation: The ferrite is in series with the common-mode loop, so $I_{cm}$ drops by $\frac{Z_{loop}+Z_f}{Z_{loop}}$ = ({{Zl|Ω}} + {{Zf|Ω}})/{{Zl|Ω}} = {{(Zl+Zf)/Zl||3}}, i.e. **{{20*log10((Zl+Zf)/Zl)||3}} dB**. Ferrites work best in low-impedance loops.

steps.prompt: A {{f0|Hz}} clock is dithered with a {{d}} % downward spread. Over what frequency range is the energy of its harmonic number {{n}} spread?
steps.explanation: Every harmonic is spread by the same **percentage**, so the absolute width grows with the harmonic number: {{n}} × {{d}} % × {{f0|Hz}} = **{{n*d/100*f0|Hz}}**. Spreading the energy over a band lowers the peak reading, typically by 10–14 dB.

steps.prompt: Which four-layer stackup (top to bottom) gives the lowest emissions?
options: Signal / Ground / Power / Signal, with thin dielectric (≤ 0.25 mm) between each signal layer and its plane
Signal / Ground / Power / Signal, all four layers equally spaced (≈ 0.5 mm)
Signal / Signal / Ground / Power
Ground / Power / Signal / Signal
steps.explanation: Every signal layer must be adjacent to a plane (Signal / Signal / Ground / Power and Ground / Power / Signal / Signal each leave one signal layer without one), and it should be tightly coupled to it: thinner dielectric means smaller loops, less plane inductance and less crosstalk. The large core between power and ground costs some interplane capacitance, which the decoupling capacitors make up for.

steps.prompt: A clock trace on layer 4 must cross the boundary between the 3.3 V and 1.8 V areas of the split power plane on layer 3. What is the best solution?
options: Reroute so it does not cross the split; if it must, add a stitching capacitor across the split right at the crossing
Make the clock trace wider where it crosses
Put a ferrite bead in series with the clock trace
Increase the drive strength of the clock buffer
steps.explanation: The return current flows in the plane under the trace; at the split it must detour to find a path, creating a large loop. Avoid the crossing, or give the return current a local high-frequency bridge with a capacitor between the two plane areas at the crossing point.

steps.prompt: Match each technique to how it reduces emissions
pairs: Spreads harmonic energy over a band
steps.explanation: Dithering changes the source and so reduces both DM and CM emissions; a ferrite only blocks common-mode current on that cable; slower edges cut all harmonics above $1/(\pi t_r)$; two symmetric return traces split the return current into two loops whose fields cancel.

steps.prompt: Halving the loop area of a clock trace also halves the common-mode radiation from the cables attached to the board.
steps.explanation: Loop area only controls differential-mode radiation (−6 dB here). Cable radiation is driven by the ground noise voltage and the common-mode current, which need ground impedance control, filtering or shielding. A dithered clock or slower edges, by contrast, reduce both.

steps.prompt: Which six-layer stackup (top to bottom) shields the high-speed signals best?
options: Signal (slow) / Ground / Signal (fast) / Signal (fast) / Power / Signal (slow)
Signal / Signal / Ground / Power / Signal / Signal
Ground / Signal / Signal / Signal / Signal / Power
steps.explanation: With Signal (slow) / Ground / Signal (fast) / Signal (fast) / Power / Signal (slow) the fast signals sit on layers 3 and 4, each next to a plane and buried between the planes. Signal / Signal / Ground / Power / Signal / Signal leaves layers 1 and 6 without an adjacent plane (not recommended); Ground / Signal × 4 / Power leaves layers 3 and 4 without an adjacent plane.

steps.prompt: A {{f0|Hz}} clock (50 % duty, $t_r$ = {{tr|s}}) drives a trapezoidal current that switches between 0 and {{I0|A}} around a {{Acm}} cm² loop. Consider its 3rd harmonic, measured at 3 m (Class B limit: 100 µV/m).

ask.prompt: Find the amplitude of the 3rd-harmonic current.
ask.explanation: $I_n = 2Id\,\frac{\sin(n\pi d)}{n\pi d}\cdot\frac{\sin(n\pi t_r/T)}{n\pi t_r/T}$ with $d$ = 0.5, $n$ = 3: $2d\,|\sin(1.5\pi)/(1.5\pi)|$ = 0.212, and the rise-time factor for $t_r/T$ = {{tr*f0||3}} is {{s3||3}}. $I_3$ = {{I0|A}} × 0.212 × {{s3||3}} = **{{I3|A}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the field strength of this harmonic in dBµV/m.
To what loop area (in cm²) must the loop shrink to just meet the limit at this harmonic?
ask.explanation: $E \propto A$: the field at {{Acm}} cm² is {{E3|V/m}}, so $A_{max}$ = {{Acm}} cm² × 100 µV/m / {{E3|V/m}} = **{{Acm*1e-4/E3||3}} cm²**.

steps.prompt: A current probe measures {{Icm|A}} of common-mode current at {{f|Hz}} on a {{L}} m cable of the same product (limit 100 µV/m at 3 m).

ask.prompt: Find the radiated field in dBµV/m.
ask.explanation: $\lambda/4$ = {{75e6/f||3}} m, longer than the cable, so $E = 12.6\times10^{-7}\frac{fLI_{cm}}{r}$ = {{E|V/m}} = **{{20*log10(E/1e-6)||3}} dBµV/m**.

ask.prompt: What minimum insertion loss (dB) must a common-mode choke on the cable give to just meet the limit?
ask.explanation: $E$ = {{E|V/m}} versus 100 µV/m: the current must drop by {{E/1e-4||3}}×, i.e. 20 log {{E/1e-4||3}} = **{{20*log10(E/1e-4)||3}} dB**. In practice add a few dB of margin.

steps.prompt: A {{L}} m cable carries {{Icm|A}} of common-mode current at {{f|Hz}}. Find the maximum field at 3 m.
steps.explanation: $\lambda/4$ = 75/{{f*1e-6||3}} MHz = {{75e6/f||3}} m is shorter than the cable, so the short-cable formula would overestimate. Use $L = \lambda/4$: $E = 12.6\times10^{-7}f\frac{\lambda}{4}\frac{I_{cm}}{r} = \frac{94.5\,I_{cm}}{r}$ = 94.5 × {{Icm|A}} / 3 = **{{94.5*Icm/3|V/m}}**, independent of length and frequency.

steps.prompt: A clock harmonic exceeds the limit by {{X}} dB. A spread-spectrum clock gives {{S}} dB reduction. By what factor must the loop area still be reduced?
steps.explanation: Remaining excess: {{X}} − {{S}} = {{X-S}} dB. $E \propto A$, so the area must shrink by $10^{{{X-S}}/20}$ = **{{10^((X-S)/20)||3}}×**.

steps.prompt: A product shows emission peaks at clock harmonics between 40 and 250 MHz that drop by 15 dB when its I/O cable is unplugged. A smaller clock loop barely helps. What is the dominant mechanism?
options: Common-mode radiation from the cable
Differential-mode radiation from the PCB loops
Conducted emission on the mains lead
Thermal noise of the line drivers
steps.explanation: The emission depends on the cable being present and is in the frequency range where common-mode radiation dominates; loop-area changes only affect differential mode. Fix: lower the ground impedance, bond circuit ground to chassis at the connector, and add a common-mode choke, filter or properly terminated shield.
